expectations.text: Identifies functional layers (detect event, identify recipients, format message, deliver, track) NOT horizontal technical layers (frontend, backend, database)
expectations.evidence: The output decomposes the feature into: Data/Persistence, Price Detection/Business Logic, Notification Delivery, User Interface/Configuration, and Scheduling/Infrastructure. These are horizontal technical layers (data tier, logic tier, delivery tier, UI tier, infra tier) rather than the functional pipeline stages the expectation demands (detect event → identify recipients → format message → deliver → track). For example, 'identify recipients' and 'format message' are absent as first-class layers; instead the output bundles concerns into technical silos. 'User Interface/Configuration' is a classic horizontal layer, not a functional step in the notification pipeline.

expectations.text: Generates at least 4 distinct options for EACH layer — not just 'simple vs complex'
expectations.evidence: Every layer contains exactly 5 options with distinct names and mechanisms: Layer 1 has in-memory map, single table, table+price_history, Redis cache, event-sourced ledger. Layer 2 has direct comparison, percentage threshold, absolute threshold, debounce/cooldown, ML anomaly detection. Layer 3 has in-app record, email, browser push, mobile push, multi-channel routing. Layer 4 has API-only, Watch button, Watch+threshold input, Watch list management page, preferences center. Layer 5 has manual script, cron job, background job queue, event-driven trigger, serverless function. All options are meaningfully distinct, not just variations of 'simple vs complex'.

expectations.text: Options within each layer follow a quality gradient from manual/hardcoded to automated/scalable
expectations.evidence: Each layer's options are ordered from simplest/most manual to most sophisticated/scalable. Examples: Layer 5 goes from 'Manual trigger (script/cURL)' → 'Cron job' → 'Background job queue' → 'Event-driven trigger' → 'Serverless scheduled function'. Layer 1 goes from 'In-memory map' → 'Single DB table' → 'Table + price_history' → 'Redis cache' → 'Event-sourced ledger'. The gradient is consistent across all five layers.

expectations.text: The proposed smallest vertical slice uses level-1 or level-2 options (manual/scripted) — NOT level-4 or level-5 options
expectations.evidence: The slice table shows: Data=option 2 (Single database table), Price Detection=option 1 (Direct comparison: current_price < last_known_price), Notification Delivery=option 2 (Email via existing transactional email service), UI=option 2 (Single 'Watch this product' button), Scheduling=option 1 (Manual trigger / cron). All selections are from the first two tiers; no level-4 or level-5 option was chosen.

expectations.text: The smallest slice is end-to-end: covers all layers, even if at the lowest quality level
expectations.evidence: The slice explicitly chooses one option for each of the five layers (Data/Persistence, Price Detection/Business Logic, Notification Delivery, User Interface/Configuration, Scheduling/Infrastructure) and describes how they work together: a user clicks Watch → a DB row is inserted → a script compares prices → an email is sent. The acceptance criteria section validates all five layers are exercisable together.

expectations.text: Proposes at least 2 follow-up slices that improve one or two layers incrementally
expectations.evidence: The output ends with a summary paragraph that says 'Subsequent iterations add sophistication layer by layer, each validated against real usage before investing in the next level of complexity' but does not define any concrete follow-up slices. No second or third slice is named, described, or composed with a layer selection table. The document has no Step 4 or follow-up slice section at all.

claims.claim: The Hamburger Method decomposes a feature by cutting horizontally through the technical stack
claims.evidence: This is actually the wrong framing. The Hamburger Method is supposed to identify functional layers (the steps in delivering value end-to-end), not technical stack layers. The model's own description of the method contradicts the intent of the skill, which calls for functional decomposition. The layers produced (Data, Business Logic, Delivery, UI, Scheduling) map to technical tiers, not functional pipeline stages.

claims.claim: A vertical slice must touch every layer
claims.evidence: The composed slice does touch all five layers as defined. The claim is internally consistent with the model's own layer definitions.

claims.claim: No new infrastructure dependencies beyond the existing database and email service
claims.evidence: The slice selects option 2 for delivery (existing email service) and option 2 for data (existing DB), and option 1/2 for scheduling (script/cron). This claim is supported by the layer choices.

claims.claim: The entire feature is observable and testable end-to-end
claims.evidence: Five acceptance criteria are listed that cover all five layers and describe observable, testable behaviors including DB state, button behavior, script execution, email content, and negative case (no email on no price change).

suggestions.assertion: Identifies functional layers (detect event, identify recipients, format message, deliver, track) NOT horizontal technical layers (frontend, backend, database)
suggestions.reason: This assertion is the most discriminating in the suite — it catches the most common failure mode (technical decomposition instead of functional decomposition). However, the example functional layers in the assertion ('detect event, identify recipients, format message, deliver, track') are generic and may not map perfectly to every domain. Consider rephrasing as 'layers correspond to pipeline steps in the value delivery flow (e.g., what triggers the notification, who receives it, what it says, how it is sent, whether it was received)' to make the criterion domain-agnostic and clearer to evaluate.

No assertion checks whether the output explicitly labels or numbers its layer options consistently (e.g., option 1 = simplest, option N = most complex). Without a numbered quality gradient, the 'level-1 or level-2' assertion in expectation 4 becomes harder to grade mechanically and easier to game by reordering options.

suggestions.assertion: Proposes at least 2 follow-up slices that improve one or two layers incrementally
suggestions.reason: This assertion is well-targeted at a genuine omission in the output. Consider also requiring that each follow-up slice specify WHICH layer(s) it upgrades and from which level to which level — this would prevent a vague mention of 'future iterations' from being miscounted as a passing slice.

eval_feedback.overall: The eval suite is well-designed: expectations 2-5 are precise and mechanically verifiable. Expectation 1 (functional vs. technical layers) is the most important discriminator and the one the model fails — that is a good catch. Expectation 6 (follow-up slices) catches a real structural gap. Main improvement area: tighten the language on 'functional layers' to reduce evaluator ambiguity, and strengthen expectation 6 to require explicit slice composition tables rather than prose mentions.
